extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and history of science; readers studying Bacon's Novum Organum and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Francis Bacon's criteria for valid scientific enquiry and for judging notions, reasoning, and methods (induction vs syllogism). Useful for evaluating scientific arguments, definitions, and method choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man as servant and interpreter of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Man, the servant and interpreter of Nature, does and understands just so much as he has discerned concerning the order of nature by observation or reflection; nor does he know more, or can he do more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge and power are limited to what has been observed or reflected upon ('re vel mente observaverit'). The passage emphasizes careful watching, registering, and interpreting of natural phenomena as the only path to knowledge or power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for instruments and auxiliaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Bare hands or unaided intellect are of limited value; things are perfected by instruments and auxiliaries needed not less for the intellect than for the hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Just as manual tools move and regulate the hand, instruments of the mind 'suggest or guard' the intellect; scientific progress requires methodological and instrumental aids, not mere unaided speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science and human power coincide
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientia et potentia humana in idem coincidunt: ignorance of cause defeats effect; nature is overcome only by obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding causes is necessary for effecting results. Knowledge (true causes) provides the rule for operation. Not all knowledge increases power; practical utility distinguishes those branches that do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human operations limited to moving natural bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Man can only move or remove natural bodies; the rest is done by Nature internally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We cannot create new substances; art combines or separates existing bodies and relies on Nature's operations—recognize the limits of human agency in experimental practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current sciences often rest on experience rather than methods of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Works already invented owe more to chance and experience than to sciences; current 'sciences' are often compilations of earlier inventions, not methods for discovering new works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing bodies of knowledge may not indicate sound methods for invention; we must develop proper methods of discovery rather than merely systematizing discovered facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of contemporary logic (syllogism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The logic in use tends to fix and promulgate errors based on vulgar notions rather than inquire into truth; syllogism constrains assent, not reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syllogistic reasoning develops consequences of principles but does not examine the principles themselves. A new logic is needed to guarantee premises as well as conclusions and to probe elementary notions and first principles via induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism unsuitable for primary principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogismus ad principia scientiarum non adhibetur; it is futile when applied to middle axioms if the subtlety of Nature exceeds it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syllogism is appropriate only after principles have been secured by induction; otherwise it merely binds assent to unclear or false premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words and notions must be clear and grounded in observation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the notions (and hence words) which are the basis of reasoning are confused and rashly abstracted from things, nothing in the superstructure will be firm; hopes rest on true induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions of natural objects or qualities should rest on prior inductions. The spoken or written word is only a symbol; unclear terms produce unsound reasoning. Form notions by observation and legitimate generalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between sound immediate notions and defective abstract notions
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple, immediate notions from sense (e.g., human, dog, warm, cold) seldom deceive; other notions used hitherto are often aberrations, ill-abstracted from things and excited improperly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer notions grounded in direct sensation where possible; beware of higher-level abstract notions and axioms that have been formed improperly by vulgar induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of forming axioms and propositions from vulgar induction
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no less desire and aberration in forming axioms than in abstracting notions; especially in first principles which depend on common (vulgar) induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors compound when axioms are derived from flawed generalisations. Induction must be rigorous to avoid propagating error through syllogistic deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two methods to inquire truth: hypothesis-first vs gradual induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Two ways exist to inquire truth: one leaps from sense and particulars to the most general axioms (often prematurely), the other ascends gradually and continuously from particulars to the most general; the latter is the true but arduous way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon recommends the gradual, ordered ascent through intermediate axioms by proper induction. The alternative (permissio intellectus or hypothesis-first) may stimulate inquiry but must be treated as provisional and subjected to rigorous inductive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissio intellectus (permissive use of the intellect/hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind, if permitted, tends to reach for more generalities and may disdain slow experience; permissive intellect (hypothesis) can make little real progress unless regulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses ('permissio intellectus') have a role as provisional devices that stimulate discovery and permit deductions to be tested against facts, but they must not be assumed true without rigorous investigation and inductive verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction should secure axioms and remedy obscure notions
rubrics_metrics.description: The office of induction is to remedy the defect of obscure, false, or inadequate notions; in forming or attempting to realize a notion we assert many propositions—sound notions require observation of facts and legitimate generalisation from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and first principles of natural objects and qualities ought always to rest on previous inductions. Induction must be the corrective to ill-defined terms and unstable principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions against acquiescence and pride in received doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind's pride and laziness, and the comforting repetition of maxims, makes people unwilling to re-examine foundations; dialectical pomposity has increased these evils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists should resist intellectual habits that favor acceptance of established principles without testing; cultivate patient, regulated inquiry and correction of 'pravo' or 'highly-embedded' mental habits through experience and experiment.
